Development guide

Tech Scan: AI workflows

Which community workflow and skill packs change how a coding agent works, and what has to be true before one of them is worth a pilot?

Draft research reference. Pack behaviour below is taken from the upstream documents and studies cited, at the versions named. No pack has been locally installed, piloted or benchmarked for this guidance. The attention scores under Research methods and historical signals come from the content-sourcing agents' scan.

Key points

  • Compare packs by approach and fit, not by rank: they solve different problems, and no pack has evidence of general superiority.
  • A pack instructs the agent; it does not enforce controls. Several packs push, merge or send code to another model provider, so read what each one does before installing it.
  • Pilot one targeted skill as well as the full pack, against the existing agent, on the same tasks.

Compare by engineering approach

Community workflow and skill packs are sets of instructions that a coding agent such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor loads so it follows particular engineering habits: interviewing you before it builds, writing a failing test first, reviewing a change from several angles, or carrying a pull request through continuous integration. Packs emphasise different approaches: composable skills you pick yourself, an end-to-end structured method, role-based review, autonomous pull-request operation, or a single set of coding principles. A pack is not the coding agent, the harness or an issue-to-PR factory.

Attention and adoption show which packs people are trying. They do not show which pack improves results, and the few published comparisons of these packs with a no-pack baseline found small or task-specific differences.[14][15] Choose by the gap in your delivery practice, by what your agent host supports, and by the permissions the pack asks for. Then measure it against your current agent before adopting. The rows below are not in rank order, and the table does not name a winner.

Seven packs by engineering approach. Each row is the pack's stated design and documented behaviour at the version named, not a measurement of productivity. The row order is not a ranking.
Pack (version read)Engineering approachWhat changes versus a plain agent runEvaluate it forTrade-off and when not to usePrerequisites and permissionsEvidence confidence
Matt Pocock skills (v1.3.2; README commit 5863806) Small, composable skills. You invoke the orchestrators. The agent may also pick up reusable disciplines. You choose skills such as /grill-me, implement and to-spec. The agent may also reach for tdd, code-review or pr. pr is the shape of a pull-request body; the review skill is code-review.[2] Requirements interrogation, domain modelling, targeted test-driven development and review. Value depends on choosing the skill. Thoughtworks, placing the library at Trial, cautions against adopting an entire skill library without evaluating the skills.[20][21] Self-updating plugin for Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot (CLI and VS Code) or Gemini CLI, or copied files for Cursor, OpenCode, Devin, Windsurf, Amp and Pi. to-spec and to-tickets write to the issue tracker you name. implement commits, after code-review.[2] Endorsement: Thoughtworks Trial, published 4 November 2026. No published comparison with a no-pack baseline was found. Low for outcomes.
Superpowers (v7.0.2) Structured method: brainstorm, then an approved design, then a plan, then strict red-green-refactor test-driven development through subagents. Skills trigger automatically (vendor statement). The agent asks before building and works test-first. After you say “go”, it can run subagents for a long stretch; the README calls a couple of hours not uncommon. That duration is the vendor's statement.[3] Complex work that needs upfront alignment, and bug fixes where you want a regression test every time. More turns, and a higher cost ratio in one small study. In a headless one-shot run, brainstorming asks questions and delivers no code.[14] A plugin per host. The README documents 16: Claude Code, Antigravity, Codex App, Codex CLI, Cursor, Devin CLI, Factory Droid, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, Grok Build CLI, Kimi Code, OpenCode, Pi, Qwen Code, Hermes Agent and Muse. A version beacon on the optional visual companion is on by default; SUPERPOWERS_DISABLE_TELEMETRY turns it off, and the project also honours Claude Code's telemetry opt-outs.[3] One independent ablation of v6.4.2 on tiny tasks: a better delivered result on 1 of 7 targeted cases, at 1.33 times the mean cost. Medium-low. A separate comparison by the author of a competing pack found small differences.[14][16]
Agent Skills, Addy Osmani (0.6.16) Broad lifecycle catalogue: 25 skills behind nine commands, from /spec to /ship. Commands route to skills, and skills also activate from context. /build auto implements a whole approved plan and commits per task. The README describes /ship as shipping to production; this page did not read that skill file, so it does not establish whether the command deploys by itself.[4] Teams that want one repeatable spec-to-ship vocabulary. Ceremony on small fixes is a sentiment recorded in the scan, not a measured result.[1] The lifecycle slash commands do not appear in GitHub Copilot. A per-skill install omits the shared references/ checklists.[4] The skills command-line installer, which the README says covers 70 or more agents, or a native plugin. Documented native setups include Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, OpenCode and Copilot CLI, with manual setup for Cursor and Windsurf. /build auto runs after one plan approval and pauses on failures or risky steps.[4] No published comparison with a no-pack baseline was found. Low for outcomes.
pstack (plugin 0.15.43) One routing skill, /poteto-mode, matches the task to a playbook. The stated aim is less code of higher quality, verified before it is called done. Planning is not a default. Opens a to-do list from a playbook, delegates to subagents, and checks the real artefact. The README says the author does not believe in planning and that code is the best spec; /poteto-mode can make a plan, but it is not the default. The skill says to name core types and data structures before writing logic.[5] Bounded, verifiable implementation, especially in Cursor. In one small Codex test, input tokens rose and the installed-but-unforced arm never invoked a pstack skill. Do not run the Shipping or Autopilot-full playbooks where a person has to approve the merge. Autopilot-stack is the same queue without the merge.[5][15] Cursor plugin (/add-plugin pstack). Claude Code installs it from the cursor/plugins marketplace; commands are prefixed, and a step that needs a Cursor-only feature is skipped. The default model panel is fable 5.2, opus 5.5 and gemini 4 carbon, changeable with /setup-pstack. Shipping and Autopilot-full can merge.[5] One practitioner report of 108 runs, with no linked dataset. Low.
gstack (1.99.5.0) Role-based sprint: office hours, plan reviews, /review, real-browser /qa and /ship. Adds specialist review passes, an outside review by a second model provider, and a local browser for QA.[6][7] Multi-perspective review and real user-interface testing. Large, and releases move quickly. Safety skills are enforced with hooks only on Claude Code. On every other host in the project's table they are advisory and do not block.[6] Claude Code is the only host the project marks as full. Its host table lists ten experimental hosts and two instruction-only hosts. Setup expects Git and Bun. Telemetry is opt-in and off by default. The update check and outside reviews are on by default; outside reviews send code, diffs or plans to a second provider under your login.[6][7] Security: a static review of version 0.4.4 (March 2026) and one published advisory for a different issue. No outcome comparison with a no-pack baseline was found. Low for outcomes.[9][10]
tstack (no release; commit 11e37a7) Pull-request lifecycle automation, plus a multi-model council review. Say “full send” and the agent proves the change, files a pull request, watches it and merges once its own gate passes. council asks models from three providers to agree. full-stop does the same work and stops before the merge.[12] Review loops, continuous-integration follow-up and pull-request hand-off. Merge authority. Where a person has to approve the merge, use full-stop or do not install full-send. full-stop still replaces project ask-first rules for test methods.[12] Claude Code or Codex. An authenticated GitHub CLI. council and sol-loop need subagents on other providers' models; sol-loop uses GPT Sol.[12] No outcome comparison was found. Low.
ub-mode (no release; commit 3da62bf) One principles skill: make it work, make it right, then follow practice, with deterministic gates. Tells the agent to write a failing test first, then hold each function under a CRAP score of 10, remove duplication at or above 0.8 similarity, and run mutation testing through companion tools. It ends by telling the agent to push to the main line.[13] Refactoring and test discipline where the companion tools fit the stack. Rigid numeric thresholds. The push step conflicts with branch-based review unless you remove it. The instruction is not evidence that branch protection can be bypassed.[13] Copy one SKILL.md. The README shows Grok, Claude and Cursor paths. Install crapper, dryer and mutator separately; the README also links uml-viewer.[13] No outcome comparison was found. Low.

Evidence confidence. Low means no published comparison with a no-pack baseline was found. Medium-low means one or two small comparisons, on a different version or on limited tasks. None of the seven packs has strong outcome evidence. Vendor descriptions of what a pack does are not measurements of whether it helps.

Match packs to lifecycle needs

Start from the gap in your current delivery practice, not from the pack. The mapping follows each pack's documented focus. It is not evidence that the pack improves that stage.[1][2][3][4][5][6][12][13]

Lifecycle need and packs that target it
NeedPacks that target it
Specify and plan before codeMatt Pocock skills (grill-me, to-spec), Superpowers (brainstorm and reviewed design), Agent Skills (/spec, /plan), pstack (data shape and foundations before logic; planning is not a default), gstack (office hours and plan reviews)
Build with less codepstack, ub-mode, Agent Skills (/build)
TestSuperpowers (strict test-driven development), Matt Pocock skills (tdd), ub-mode (test-driven development with complexity, duplication and mutation gates), gstack (browser QA), Agent Skills (/test)
Reviewtstack (multi-model council), gstack (review and security roles), Superpowers (review against the plan), pstack (verify against the real artefact before “done”), Matt Pocock skills (code-review), Agent Skills (/review)
Ship and learngstack (/ship), tstack (full-send and full-stop), pstack (Shipping and Autopilot-full), Agent Skills (/ship; whether that command deploys was not established), ub-mode (push to the main line), Matt Pocock skills (retro). Read Bound autonomy before using any ship step

Packs overlap. Superpowers, Matt Pocock's skills, Agent Skills and ub-mode each include a test-driven development routine, and five include a review step: Superpowers, Matt Pocock's skills, gstack, tstack and Agent Skills. pstack's check is to verify the real artefact before calling the work done. Combining packs loads more instructions at once. The scan records practitioners pairing parts of packs, for example Matt Pocock's skills with tstack's council.[1] In SkillsBench, tasks given four or more skills gained less than tasks given one to three, but those were curated skills written for the benchmark's tasks, not these packs, so the difference is a reason to pilot a combination rather than evidence that combining these packs helps or hurts.[17] Treat any combination as its own pilot arm. For spec artefacts and work tracking, see Workflows & factories.

Read the evidence

Three kinds of evidence answer different questions. Do not use one of them as a substitute for the others.

Attention and adoption: who is trying it. Launch-week posts, Hacker News threads, install counts and marketplace listings show interest, and they favour large audiences and new launches. The content-sourcing agents' scan measured these in October and November 2026 and found that attention and sustained adoption ranked the packs very differently.[1] A Thoughtworks Radar ring is an informed opinion, not a test result. The 4 November 2026 edition places mattpocock/skills at Trial and, in the same blip, cautions against adopting entire skill libraries without evaluating them. The same edition places agent skill cognitive surrender at Caution.[20][21] GitHub stars are not usage and are not used here as evidence.

Outcomes: does it change results. Few comparisons with a no-pack baseline exist, and each is small. Read the scope beside the number.

  • An independent ablation by Bartłomiej Krupa (29 September 2026) ran Superpowers v6.4.2 against no plugin, using Claude Code's plugin eval. There were 12 cases (7 positive, 4 negative, 1 control) on tiny Node projects, 8 runs per arm (192 scored runs), with Claude Sonnet 5.5 as both agent and judge. The plugin improved the delivered result on 1 of the 7 positive cases. On that bug fix it added a regression test in 8 of 8 runs, against 4 of 8 without the plugin. It also changed process elsewhere, including test-first work and asking questions instead of building on a vague request. The mean of the 12 per-case cost ratios was 1.33 times (range 1.08 to 1.63). The author's limits: small tasks only; long multi-step work, subagents and worktrees were not tested; one model and one plugin version; the judge was the same model family. In a headless one-shot run, brainstorming asks and hands back nothing to run. This is not a refutation of multi-stage workflows on larger work, and it does not test v7.0.2. Cases and transcripts are published with the article.[14]
  • A practitioner, Cici (@LabubuNoBB), reported 108 Codex runs on 4 November 2026: 12 frozen cases, 3 runs, 3 arms (no pstack; pstack installed but not forced; the prompt forces poteto-mode). Pass rates were 36/36, 35/36 and 34/36, which the post calls not significant, and the post says the failures in the second and third arms had correct code but omitted a function name from the final report. Input tokens were 24% higher in the installed arm and 75% higher when the prompt forced the skill. In the installed-only arm, no pstack skill was invoked in 36 runs. Added tests fell from 7 to 3, and tests that catch the old bug from 7 of 15 to 3 of 15. Stated limits: n=3, one model, which the post does not name, small single-file tasks, and multi-agent work off. The post says multi-file work was not tested. No repository, dataset or write-up is linked, so the result has not been independently reproduced. It is a reported small test, not a causal finding beyond those tasks.[15]
  • Utkarsh (@utk0x) reported 267 runs on 25 September 2026: all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, once each, under three set-ups in Claude Code with Gemini 3.6 Flash High. The author's own pack, Supreme, solved 61, three more than Superpowers and six more than a no-prompt baseline. Paired McNemar tests did not clear a 0.05 threshold: p = 0.605 against Superpowers and p = 0.239 against the baseline. A Superpowers-versus-baseline test is not reported. On 14 esoteric and symbolic tasks the no-prompt baseline scored highest, 12 of 14. The author built the competing pack, so this is a comparison with a conflict of interest. Use it only as evidence that results vary by task and that the differences here were small.[16]

Broader research points the same way, with a narrower kind of skill. SkillsBench v4 (14 June 2026) ran 87 tasks across 8 domains under 18 model–harness configurations, including OpenHands, Gemini CLI, Claude Code and Codex CLI. Curated skills raised the average pass rate from 33.9% to 50.5% (16.6 percentage points). Software-engineering tasks gained 11.6 percentage points (37.6% to 49.2%, 16 tasks). Tasks paired with one skill gained 18.0 percentage points, tasks with two or three gained 19.0, and tasks with four or more gained 10.1. On three harness configurations, skills the agent wrote itself landed below the no-skills baseline. Thirteen of the 87 tasks had a negative change. These are curated skills written for the benchmark's tasks. They are not the general workflow packs on this page, so the gains are not evidence that any of those packs has the same effect.[17]

Fit: will it work here. That depends on the host, the permission model and the task mix in the comparison above. Only a local pilot can answer it for a team. Vendor install lists and marketplace listings are discovery signals, not evidence of task success.

A 16 November 2026 scan assigned each pack an analyst-assigned ecosystem evidence score from 0 to 100, using small samples of opinion posts and unequal adoption proxies. Ranks 3 to 5 are effectively tied, and tstack and ub-mode were about three weeks old when scored. The scores are an analyst's judgement against small samples, not a measurement of productivity, and they are not a shortlist.[1]

Research methods and historical signals (16 November 2026)

These scores were assigned by the content-sourcing agents from small samples (8 to 25 opinion posts per pack) and unequal adoption proxies on 16 November 2026. The scan called the composite an industry acceptance score. It is recorded here as an analyst-assigned ecosystem evidence score. It describes ecosystem attention and endorsement, not effectiveness or quality, and it is not a recommendation order. The cautions are the scan's summaries; Bound autonomy and the outcome list above correct the permission and benchmark wording.[1]

Ranks 3 to 5 are effectively tied, and tstack and ub-mode were about three weeks old when scored. The scores are an analyst's judgement against small samples, not a measurement of productivity.[1]

Viral index. For each pack, take the top three original, on-topic, non-repost X posts in the window. Post engagement is likes + 2 × reposts + 2 × quotes + replies + 0.5 × bookmarks; the pack score is the sum of the three. The index is 100 × score ÷ the top score (pstack, 38,610). Impressions, mention counts and GitHub stars were reported separately and are not part of the index. The search was relevancy-ranked with at most 25 results per query, so it is a sample, not a census.

Acceptance score. Each pack was scored 1–10 on five dimensions: sentiment (25%), breadth (20%), sustained adoption (25%), independent endorsement (20%) and maturity (10%); the composite is 10 × the weighted sum. Inputs included hand-coded X samples excluding the author's own posts, Hacker News threads, a Reddit archive, GitHub activity, CLI install counts, official marketplace listings and independent reviews such as the Thoughtworks Technology Radar. With equal weights the order holds, except that pstack and gstack tie.[1]

The content-sourcing agents' scan ranked seven packs by a viral index: engagement on the top three X posts for each pack between 15 October and 12 November 2026, with X-post leads supplied by Grok Bot. A follow-up acceptance pass on 16 November 2026 scored the same packs for what it called industry acceptance: independent sentiment, breadth of discussion, sustained adoption, independent endorsement and maturity. The two largely disagree. The viral index rewards large audiences and packs launched inside the window; the acceptance score rewards sustained use and independent validation. Neither score is a reason to adopt a pack.[1]

  • Matt Pocock skills. The scan says developers value aligning the agent before it writes code and skills that stay small and composable. Concerns recorded there: overkill on simple work, skills that do not fire automatically, and adopting whole libraries without evaluation. Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed the library at Trial on 4 November 2026; that is an endorsement signal, not a task result.[20]
  • Superpowers. The scan calls this the largest and most divided discussion: valued for a reviewed design before code, strict test-driven development and long unattended runs, and criticised for token and context consumption and a reported v7 regression. The regression complaint is scan sentiment, not a defect re-tested here.
  • Agent Skills. The scan says it is valued for spec-first ordering, evidence gates and browser and web-performance skills, and criticised as ceremony for one-line fixes.
  • pstack. The scan reports the warmest independent sentiment, a single /poteto-mode entry point, and concerns about token use. It ships in Cursor's marketplace and also installs in Claude Code from the cursor/plugins repository.[5]
  • gstack. The scan calls it the most polarised: valued for its structured sprint and browser QA, criticised for bloat and for telemetry. Telemetry in version 1.99.5.0 is opt-in and off by default; see Bound autonomy.[7]
  • tstack. The scan reports positive but thin early sentiment, mainly for council reviews, and no Hacker News threads at the time of the analysis. That absence was not re-checked for this revision.
  • ub-mode. The scan says it is valued for deterministic quality gates and criticised for rigid metric targets. Reports that the companion tools were hard to find, or that one crashed, are practitioner reports in the scan. The README at commit 3da62bf links crapper, dryer, mutator and uml-viewer.[1][13]

Bound autonomy

A pack instructs the agent; it does not enforce permissions, branch protection, sandboxing or release approval. Those stay in repository settings, continuous integration and the host's permission mode. Several packs include steps that push, merge or send work to another provider. The versions below are the ones read for this page.

Plugin pins. A pin protects you only if the installer checks it. Claude Code before 2.1.179 could install a branch named like the pinned commit; verify the installed commit after installing a pack as a plugin. [23]

Merging. tstack's full-send applies only when you explicitly say “full send”. It then grants the agent permission to merge once its own gate passes: the proof covers the diff, required checks are green, review bots have finished and each finding is fixed or dismissed with a written reason, no human review still requests changes, and the branch is up to date and mergeable. It says to merge through branch protection as configured, and not to use --admin or other bypasses. It also says the agent can ignore automated reviews that request “needs human review” when it has high confidence. full-stop does the same work, never merges, turns off existing auto-merge, and will not enter a merge queue or push to the default branch.[12] pstack's Shipping playbook lands a contiguous run of verified pull requests, through the GitHub CLI by default or Origin when that CLI is available. Autopilot-full runs a queue of independent pull requests through to merge after a verifier swarm, which did not write the code, has checked each one. Autopilot-stack stops before the merge. The playbook says passing continuous integration on its own never authorises a merge, and items the operator keeps as their own stop at merge-ready.[5]

Overriding project rules. On that explicit “full send” or “full stop” trigger, tstack replaces project-file rules that say to ask before a test method, including computer use, browser automation, simulators, running the app or a dev server, screenshots and visual checks. The same permission is in full-stop. Neither skill overrides a harness or system approval prompt if one appears, and full-send says the testing permission does not extend to production changes or deleting data.[12] If an ask-first rule in AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md exists for safety rather than convenience, remove these skills or enforce the rule in the host's permission settings. A line in those files does not block the skill.

Pushing. gstack's /ship, at version 1.99.5.0, is titled a fully automated ship workflow. Its description says it merges the base, runs tests, reviews the diff, bumps the version and changelog, pushes and creates a pull request. Routine work needs no confirmation, including uncommitted changes, the version choice, the changelog draft and commits. It stops at stated gates. For a complex or ambiguous merge conflict it stops and asks before any edit.[11] ub-mode's practice section says “Push to the main line at the end.” That is an instruction to the agent. It is not evidence that a protected branch can be bypassed.[13] Configure branch protection if a push to the main line is not acceptable. Neither instruction replaces that setting.

Long unattended runs. Superpowers can run subagents after design approval; the couple-of-hours claim is the vendor's.[3] Agent Skills' /build auto implements a whole approved plan and commits per task, pausing on failures or risky steps.[4]

Data leaving the machine. gstack separates three switches. Usage telemetry is opt-in and off by default; on first run it asks once, and gstack-config set telemetry off turns it off. When on, it sends the skill name, outcome, duration, version, operating system and similar fields to gstack's Supabase, and the privacy note says code, file paths, repository and branch names, and prompts are never sent. An update check runs at every interactive skill start, on by default whatever the telemetry setting: GitHub requests only, plus version and operating system to Supabase if telemetry is on. Turn it off with gstack-config set update_check false. Outside reviews are on by default. The first send prints a notice naming the provider and account. Plan reviews, /autoplan, /review, /ship passes, design review, office hours, /spec and others can send the review prompt and the relevant code, diff or plan to a second provider (Codex under Claude Code, Claude Code under Codex) using your own login. Turn them off with gstack-config set codex_reviews disabled. Each gstack-initiated off-machine send writes a hash-chained local receipt (gstack-egress list). The project calls that an audit trail, not a network firewall.[7] tstack's council and pstack's default model panel send work to models from several providers.[5][12] Superpowers loads a version beacon by default unless disabled.[3] The READMEs read for Matt Pocock's skills, Agent Skills and ub-mode do not describe telemetry. That is not a code audit. Check each path against your data-handling rules before use.

Host differences. gstack enforces its safety skills with hooks only on Claude Code, the only host it marks as full. On the other hosts in its table the safety skills are advisory and not blocked. The project calls “full” its own certification by a workflow run, not an independent certification.[6]

Security history. A static review by Redeux Security (RDXS-2026-007, published 16 March 2026) of gstack 0.4.4, commit c86faa7, reported two server issues: unauthenticated cookie-picker routes on the local browser daemon, and a project-local bearer-token file that any process of the same user could read. As design observations, which the review says are not vulnerabilities, it noted that /qa edited code and committed with no human review gate, and that /ship committed, pushed and opened a pull request under a prompt the review quotes as telling the agent not to ask for confirmation. No running instance was attacked.[10] gstack's changelog records later cookie-picker changes: 0.13.1.0 (28 March 2026) required a bearer token on the data routes; 0.15.7.0 (5 April 2026) made that authentication mandatory; 0.16.1.0 (8 April 2026) replaced a token in the HTML with a one-time code exchanged for an HttpOnly session cookie, crediting a CVSS 7.8 report. The current code comment calls this an authentication model after a CVE fix: a one-time code with a five-minute lifetime or a session cookie with a one-hour lifetime for the page, and a bearer token or session cookie for the data routes. The changelog and the comment do not give a CVE identifier. This is upstream's documented remediation, not an independent re-test of version 1.99.5.0.[8] The repository's only published GitHub advisory is a different issue, GHSA-249x-w96r-pw6c (high, published 20 October 2026, no CVE identifier): gstack before 1.91.159.0 applied a repository's .env and bunfig.toml preload to gstack's Bun processes. It was fixed in 1.91.159.0.[9]

In one practitioner's small Codex test, 12 single-file tasks with 3 runs and 3 arms, pstack showed no significant pass-rate gain and used more input tokens. The model is not named, multi-file work was not tested, and no dataset is published.[15] Treat every pack as an experiment to measure, not a productivity upgrade.

Keep protected branches, independent continuous integration, task-scoped credentials and an authorised human merge and release decision outside the pack, as set out in Workflows & factories and Delivery. Remove or deny any skill that merges, pushes to a protected branch or deploys. Run packs in the sandbox and permission mode you would use without them.

Pilot before adoption

The engineering lead picks one lifecycle gap and runs three arms on the same bounded, representative tasks. Arm A is the no-pack baseline: the existing agent set-up with no pack. Arm B is the single most relevant skill from the pack. Arm C is the full pack. Keep the model, host version, starting context, repository state and acceptance tests identical, and repeat each task several times. Agent runs vary. The published comparisons used 3 to 8 runs per arm, and Claude Code's plugin eval runs each case three times by default and reports the with-plugin score, the without-plugin score and the difference. If a case scores 1.0 both ways, the plugin is not what made it pass.[14][15][18] OpenAI's guide for Codex skills, published 22 January 2026, says to define outcome, process, style and efficiency goals, to check that the skill triggers, and that a set of 10 to 20 prompts is enough to surface regressions.[19] The single-skill arm shows whether a small addition gets the benefit without the full pack's cost. SkillsBench found that focused skills gained more than large bundles, on curated task skills rather than these packs.[17] Treat the result as a local pilot, not general productivity proof. Keep independent human review before merge, and see Verification for evidence.

Check before adoption

  • Pack pinned to a reviewed commit or version; licence and installer reviewed.
  • Arm A verified clean: no pack files, hooks, plugins or memory leaking into the no-pack baseline. One practitioner reported a baseline that could read a skill pack through file reads the sandbox did not stop, and voided 3 of 6 paired runs on that kind of check.[22] Arm B has only the one skill and any files it needs.
  • Same model, host version, context, tasks and acceptance tests in all arms; several runs per task.
  • Merge, push-to-main and deploy steps removed or denied by repository settings. Ask-first rules you depend on are enforced in the host, not only in AGENTS.md.
  • Permission mode, sandbox and credentials unchanged from the no-pack baseline.
  • Telemetry, update checks, outside reviews and multi-provider model calls listed and approved, or turned off.
  • Recorded per arm: pass rate on hidden acceptance tests, regressions, regression tests added, review interventions, rework, elapsed time, tokens, data sent off the machine, and any permission or approval deviations.
  • Whether the skill actually fired in each run. In one test, an installed pack was never invoked.[15]

Record the expected and observed results and any unresolved failure before widening use.

Gaps and refresh

The scan's samples are small (8 to 25 opinion posts per pack), engagement-farming accounts are common, and names such as “pstack”, “tstack” and “superpowers” collide with unrelated uses. Install counts depend on the channel: command-line counts miss marketplace and custom installers. GitHub stars are not usage and are not used here as evidence. Some figures in the scan are author claims. Each cited outcome comparison is small and tests a single model, and the pstack comparison has no published dataset.[1][14][15][16]

Whether Agent Skills' /ship deploys by itself was not read from the skill file. Whether Matt Pocock's skills, Agent Skills, pstack, tstack or ub-mode send telemetry was not established by a code audit; only the READMEs and skill files cited here were read. gstack's cookie-picker fixes are the project's changelog and code comments, not a fresh attack against version 1.99.5.0. The Utkarsh comparison's repository was not opened. No local pilot has been run for this page.

Adjacent trends seen in the same window were not scored because they are platforms or methods rather than skill packs, including “harness engineering”; see Harness. Recheck a pack's entry when any of these happens: a new security advisory or fix; a change to default permissions, telemetry, the update check or outside-review defaults; a new merge, push or deploy step; a change in supported hosts; a major version; or a new published comparison with a no-pack baseline. gstack's version-specific claims go out of date fastest, because it releases several times a week. The scan's attention and adoption signals can still be refreshed monthly; refreshing them does not by itself decide adoption.[1]
